articles.title: Friend backs Springhill Hospice Christmas appeal after Leanne Field’s last Minions party
articles.excerpt: Sally Kerr is backing Springhill Hospice’s Christmas appeal in memory of her best friend Leanne Field, 45, who had one last party at the Rochdale hospice two days before she died.
articles.content_html:
The best friend of a woman who spent her final days at Rochdale’s Springhill Hospice is backing its Christmas appeal in her memory.

Leanne Field, 45, was diagnosed with metastatic sarcoma, a rare type of cancer, in 2021. After time in hospital, she moved into the hospice on Broad Lane at the end of August.

Hospice staff helped her have one last party, surrounded by the people who loved her most, all dressed as Minions, her favourite characters.

The party was held on Saturday 5 September. Leanne died two days later, on Monday 7 September.

Her friend Sally Kerr, 47, of Shaw, who works with Manchester FA, said: “She got admitted to the hospice and originally, it was for symptom management. She’d been in hospital, but it wasn’t the best environment so all we wanted to do was get her in a hospice because I’ve been to hospices before and I have an understanding of what you get, it’s next level and I knew it’d be better for her.”

“We all knew the end was close, but we weren’t ready to say goodbye just yet,” Ms Kerr said.

The pair met in 1998, almost 28 years ago. Ms Kerr said: “I met her at a rave, she loved raving. She danced everywhere, she’d make up a dance to anything. She was just a real character, she was loyal, she was fierce. She was passionate, if you had her love, you had everything. She was just a really good human being.”

Of Leanne’s love of Minions, she said: “She was obsessed she had them all over the house. Everything started going yellow, her tracksuit, trainers, she just loved it. She was a massive kid.”

Ms Kerr said that despite Leanne’s medication and tiredness, her hand began to move when one of her favourite songs was played at the party.

“When one of her songs came on, she was in her wheelchair, and you could just see her revving, and I thought there’s the song, there you go,” she said.

“It meant the world because ultimately, we wanted the opportunity to listen to our music together and to have a little bit of a laugh. You just want that one last time. We wanted Leanne to see that we were still there for her, we wanted her to see she had her girls no matter what.”

Speaking about the hospice, she said: “It’s massive, it’s a big thing. They make it easier and personal, they give you the privacy, and they give you the amenities to spend more time with your loved one. Everything is specific to your loved one in a hospice.”

This will be Ms Kerr’s first Christmas without Leanne. She said: “Without them we wouldn’t have got the memories that we got. It made our last memories with Leanne a little bit better.”

She is urging people across the borough to support the appeal so other families can make similar memories.

“We were all desperate for time with Leanne because your time is not promised. Without the Hospice our last memories would have been going to a hospital. That’s not the environment where we wanted our last memories to be, we wanted her to have the best and be with us,” she said.

Springhill says it is facing increasing demand for its services alongside rising running costs, which have gone up by £2 million in the past five years. The hospice relies on support from the community to keep its services going.

Donations to the Christmas appeal can be made through Springhill Hospice’s website at www.springhill.org.uk/event/christmas-appeal-2026/.

Source: Springhill Hospice press office, press release issued on 16 November 2026. Image: Springhill Hospice / supplied.

articles.title: Seven Sisters to be demolished as RBH plans around 600 new homes at College Bank
articles.excerpt: All seven College Bank tower blocks will come down, with a planning application for around 600 new homes expected in early 2027. RBH expects every remaining customer to have moved out by summer 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks at College Bank are to be demolished and replaced with around 600 new homes, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has decided.

The RBH Board made the decision after more than a year of work with partners in the College Bank Task Force and a review of all available options. RBH will now seek planning approval.

A planning application for the redevelopment is expected to go to Rochdale Borough Council in early 2027. RBH hopes to build a mix of apartment blocks and town houses on the site.

A feasibility study carried out in summer 2025 found that keeping and refurbishing the seven 1960s blocks would cost at least £269 million and take up to 12 years.

RBH said refurbished flats would last around 50 years, while newly built homes are expected to last significantly longer.

Of the 766 flats across the seven blocks, 78 households have yet to accept an offer of a new home. Rehousing will continue, and RBH expects every customer to have moved out by summer 2027.

RBH chief executive Amanda Newton said: "Today marks an important step forward for College Bank and for the future of housing in Rochdale."

She added: "College Bank has been home to generations of Rochdalians, and we recognise the important place the blocks hold in many people's memories."

"This decision gives us a way forward together and allows us to focus on the opportunities ahead," Ms Newton said.

The College Bank Task Force is chaired by the Mayor of Greater Manchester. Its members include the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and Rochdale Borough Council.

Demolition was first proposed in 2017, when RBH warned the blocks were nearing the end of their useful life. Those plans would have taken down four towers, Mitchell Hey, Dunkirk Rise, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow, and refurbished Underwood, Mardyke and Holland Rise.

Tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign in response. They hoped RBH's partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the blocks restored, but that partnership was announced as ending in September 2024.

Residents began moving out in October 2025, after RBH raised concerns about the long-term safety of the blocks. RBH, which has more than 12,000 customers across the borough, says the decision also lets it keep investing in homes elsewhere.

RBH is holding sessions for customers on Wednesday 18 November: at Spotland Community Centre, 92-96 Spotland Road, from 2.30pm to 3.30pm and 4pm to 5pm, and at the Town Mill Brow Community Room, College Bank, from 5.30pm to 6.30pm.

Regular drop-ins continue at the Town Mill Brow Community Room on Tuesdays from 1pm to 4pm and Thursdays from 3pm to 6pm. Residents can also email towncentre.regen@rbh.org.uk or call 0800 027 7769.

articles.title: Demolition of Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks confirmed
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has announced plans to demolish the Seven Sisters tower blocks, paving the way for new housing developments.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed plans to demolish the iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks, known as College Bank, marking a significant change in the landscape of Rochdale.

The decision follows a decade of uncertainty regarding the future of the buildings, which have been largely vacant for some time.

The demolition will pave the way for approximately 600 new homes, including a mix of apartment blocks and townhouses.

RBH's chief executive, Amanda Newton, stated that this decision represents an important step forward for the College Bank area and aims to address the current and future housing needs of Rochdale residents.

Newton expressed gratitude to the community for their patience throughout the lengthy process, acknowledging the historical significance of the Seven Sisters to many local residents. She noted, "This decision gives us a way forward together and allows us to focus on the opportunities ahead."

The Seven Sisters, built in the 1960s, have been deemed too costly to refurbish, with estimates suggesting a £269 million price tag and a 12-year timeline for renovations.

Currently, only 78 of the 766 flats are occupied, prompting RBH to begin relocating residents in October 2025, with all expected to be moved out by summer 2027.

  • Currently, only 78 of the 766 flats are occupied, prompting RBH to begin relocating residents in October 2025, with all expected to be moved out by summer 2027.

articles.title: Join for a Toy membership launched to support Rochdale Christmas Toy Appeal
articles.excerpt: Your Trust Rochdale has launched a new membership initiative called Join for a Toy, aimed at supporting this year's Christmas Toy Appeal. The initiative encourages community members to donate suitable gifts for children and families in need across the borough during the festive season.
articles.content_html:
Your Trust Rochdale has launched a membership initiative called Join for a Toy to support this year's Christmas Toy Appeal, encouraging donations of suitable gifts for children and families in need across the borough.

To participate, individuals must donate a new, unwrapped toy suitable for children aged 0 to 16 years when purchasing their membership. This initiative aims to collect toys for local families who may struggle to provide gifts this Christmas.

Memberships must be purchased in person at any leisure centre, and donors are reminded to bring a suitable toy with them.

For more information about the initiative, visit Your Trust Rochdale's website.

What it means for Rochdale

  • Memberships must be purchased in person at leisure centres with a toy donation.
  • To participate, individuals must donate a new, unwrapped toy suitable for children aged 0 to 16 years when purchasing their membership.

articles.title: Students trained as Rochdale Creative Health Advocates at Falinge Park High School
articles.excerpt: Students from various schools participated in training to become Creative Health Advocates, aimed at promoting health and wellbeing in the community.
articles.content_html:
Students from multiple schools participated in training last week to become Rochdale Creative Health Advocates at Falinge Park High School. The initiative aims to empower young people to promote health and wellbeing within their communities.

The training focused on equipping students with skills to advocate for health-related issues, encouraging them to take an active role in improving the wellbeing of their peers and families. This programme is part of a broader effort to engage youth in community health initiatives.

Falinge Park High School has been instrumental in facilitating this training, providing resources and support to ensure students are well-prepared for their roles as advocates. The school aims to foster a sense of responsibility and leadership among its students.

This initiative aligns with ongoing efforts to enhance community health in Rochdale, encouraging young people to contribute positively to their environment. The next steps include further training sessions and opportunities for students to engage with local health projects.

articles.title: 215th anniversary of Rochdale statesman John Bright's birth celebrated
articles.excerpt: Today marks 215 years since the birth of John Bright, a key figure in free trade and abolitionism, who was born in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Today marks the 215th anniversary of the birth of John Bright, a prominent Rochdale-born statesman known for his advocacy of free trade and abolitionism.

Bright, who lived from 1811 to 1889, is celebrated as one of Rochdale's greatest figures, having earned admiration from notable contemporaries including Abraham Lincoln and Lord Salisbury.

John Bright was a member of the Radical Party before its merger into the Liberal Party in 1859. He served as an MP for four different constituencies and held cabinet positions under Prime Minister William Gladstone.

His commitment to social justice included supporting the abolition of slavery and advocating for the rights of the working class.

Bright was instrumental in the Anti-Corn Law League, which he co-founded with Richard Cobden. Their efforts led to the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, a significant shift towards free trade that benefitted the urban working class by lowering food prices.

This was a controversial move, with critics arguing it harmed British agriculture, yet it marked a pivotal moment in British economic policy.

Two statues of John Bright stand in Greater Manchester, one near Manchester Town Hall and another in Broadfield Park, Rochdale. Both were unveiled in 1891, with the Rochdale statue inscribed as 'Rochdale's greatest townsman'.

Bright's legacy continues to be celebrated, reflecting his profound impact on British politics and social reform.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Today marks 215 years since the birth of the 'greatest master of English oratory' John Bright, influential Rochdale-born statesman | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch Today marks 215 years since the birth of the 'greatest master of English oratory' John Bright, influential Rochdale-born statesman JS Jack Shepherd Junior Reporter November 16, 2026 | 1 hour ago Print Today marks the 215th anniversary of the birth of the free-trade advocate and abolitionist John Bright (1811-1889). Celebrated and lauded by many, including Abraham Lincoln and Lord Salisbury, John Bright is arguably Rochdale's greatest statesman John Bright was a statesman from Rochdale, belonging initially to the Radical Party until its merger into the Liberal Party in 1859. He was lauded by many, Lord Salisbury, former Prime Minister three times over, upon Bright's death, remarked that "he (Bright) was the greatest master of English oratory that this generation has produced, or I may perhaps say several generations back." Abraham Lincoln had a portrait of John Bright in his office, and among the items retrieved from his pocket upon his assassination, was a testimony from Bright supporting the re-election of the President. Bright became an MP for 4 separate constituencies, and served as a cabinet minister on three separate occasions, all under Liberal Prime Minister William Gladstone. Bright was an abolitionist, and supported fugitive slave Frederick Douglass both spread his story, and become a free man. Bright was a supporter of the co-operative movement, and introduced Douglass to crowds almost a thousand strong in Rochdale wanting to hear him speak of his story as a slave in America. Frederick Douglass notably spoke in the Public Room on Baillie Street on October 10th 1846, just a three minute walk from where the first co-operative store was opened by the Rochdale Pioneers two years prior. Bright contributed a third of the cost to buy Douglass' freedom from slavery, and, in 1847, Douglass went back to America a free man. Douglass was a regular guest at 'One Ash', the home of John Bright, and he stayed there the night before he was to leave England for America as a free man for the first time. Douglass noted that, relating to the hospitality of Bright “I was, besides, a welcome guest at the home of Mr. Bright in Rochdale and treated as a friend and brother among his brothers and sisters.” Douglass went on to become an influential abolitionist and supporter of women's suffrage, being the only black attendant to the first women's rights convention, and the first black candidate for the vice-presidency under the first female candidate for the presidency. Bright was known for his staunch advocacy for free-trade policies, evidenced through his role in the Anti-Corn Law League, which he founded alongside his friend (and later MP for Rochdale) Richard Cobden. The Corn Laws were a set of mercantilist/protectionist tariffs and trade restrictions levied on imported wheat in an attempt to protect national farming interests. This caused the prices for common wheat products like bread to rise, disproportionately negatively impacting the urban working class. Bright joined forces with Cobden with the creation of one of the first nationwide successful pressure groups, officially in 1836, but functionally in 1838. In 1846, the Conservative Prime Minister Robert Peel led the successful battle for repeal, and the success of the pressure group established by Bright and Cobden was a primary reason for the eventual repealing of these laws, symbolising a shift in policy from mercantilism/protectionism to free trade. This was incredibly controversial, and the conservatives broadly didn't support this, with Peel relying on the support of the Whigs to pass the repeal of the Corn Laws. Peel resigned the very day that the repeal passed through parliament. Critics of the repeal of the Corn Laws, including Benjamin Disraeli, saw that the repeal of these laws caused the ruin of British agriculture, yet supporters of the repeal of these laws saw that the urban working class were baring an unfair load as a result of the expensive food prices. Benjamin Disraeli opted not to reinstate the Corn Laws for this reason, seeing the value of free-trade policies and the benefit that the repeal of the law had on the urban working class. Rochdale statesman John Bright, and former Rochdale MP Richard Cobden were two of the main pioneers for the repeal of the Corn Laws, and of the extension of free-trade policies in Britain. Two famous terms have been attributed to Bright, one being the idiom to 'flog a dead horse', and the other being in relation to England being the 'mother of all parliaments'. Bright has two statues, one near Manchester Town Hall, and the other in Broadfield Park in Rochdale. They were both unveiled in 1891, but the latter was moved from the initial placing of the Town Hall Square to the park in 1933. The inscriptions on the statue in Broadfield Park note Bright as 'Rochdale's greatest townsman', accompanied by quotes from the 'master of English oratory'. The recent renovation to Rochdale Town Hall, when it re-opened in March 2024, included the renovation of room previously created to house Rochdale's first Free Library, which suffered as a result of a fire in 1883. That room is now named after John, The Bright Hall, and is available for hire. The Quaker burial ground in Ball Street Gardens is where Bright rests, along with his brother Jacob Bright, the first Mayor of Rochdale, his mother, father, sister, and second wife. articles.title: Decision made on future of College Bank towers in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing plans to replace the Seven Sisters with 600 new homes following a decision to demolish the iconic structures.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed the demolition of the Seven Sisters, also known as College Bank, after a lengthy decision-making process lasting ten years.

The decision to demolish the Seven Sisters was made due to the high costs associated with refurbishing the 1960s blocks, which were deemed unfeasible.

RBH plans to submit a planning application for redevelopment in early 2027, aiming to create a mix of apartment blocks and townhouses to replace the iconic structures.

The College Bank Task Force collaborated with RBH throughout this process, acknowledging the significance of the Seven Sisters in the community's memories while focusing on future housing opportunities.

The demolition will pave the way for approximately 600 new homes, marking an important step for housing development in Rochdale.

The Seven Sisters were first earmarked for demolition a decade ago, and this decision allows RBH to concentrate on new housing initiatives in the area.

What it means for Rochdale

  • RBH plans to submit a planning application for redevelopment in early 2027.
  • The demolition will allow for the construction of around 600 new homes.
  • Residents can expect a mix of apartment blocks and townhouses in the future.

articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has announced enhanced support for homeless individuals in the borough as winter temperatures begin to fall. The initiative aims to provide additional resources and assistance to those experiencing homelessness during the colder months.

To combat the effects of severe weather, the council is closely monitoring temperatures and deploying extra outreach workers to help those sleeping rough. These workers will engage with individuals in need, offering support and guidance on available services.

Support hubs have been established across the borough, providing access to hot food and drinks for those in need. The council is also collaborating with the Safe Haven to ensure that individuals requiring accommodation receive the necessary assistance during this critical time.

The increased support measures are part of the council's ongoing commitment to prevent homelessness and provide essential services to vulnerable residents. As winter progresses, the council will continue to adapt its approach to meet the needs of the community.

Published: 16 November 2026 People experiencing homelessness across Rochdale borough are being provided with extra support as the cold weather sweeps in. Temperatures are closely monitored and, when severe weather conditions are forecast, the support already available to people sleeping rough significantly increases across all townships. Additional outreach workers are now on the streets during the day and throughout the night, engaging with anyone sleeping rough and helping them access accommodation and support services. Bed capacity across accommodation services has been increased, while community support hubs will extend their opening hours during periods of severe weather. The hubs provide access to hot food and drinks, shower and laundry facilities, welfare support, health services and more to help people move away from rough sleeping and into longer-term accommodation. In addition, housing staff will continue to link in with the new Safe Haven site in Rochdale Town Hall Square. The Safe Haven is a trailer which parks in this area every Saturday between 10pm and 3am and is fully staffed with clinical and non-clinical teams to support anyone who is on a night out and feeling vulnerable. The teams supporting the homeless, including the council and its many partners, will continue to work with the safe haven team to ensure that anyone who is going into the haven because they need a bed for the night will be supported into accommodation. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration, said: “Council teams and partners work all year round to support our most vulnerable residents, but we know they are more at risk in cold weather. By significantly stepping up the support at this time of year, we will ensure that nobody who wants a bed will be without one. “This 24-hour response supports people in immediate crisis and that’s really important, but we also offer long term support because ultimately, we want people to be able to build a life away from the streets. As well as provision to help the person, like support with jobs, training and mental health, we’re also creating new move-on accommodation to help people who are working towards a permanent home, and in the longer term are working to create more affordable housing.” Anyone who sees a person on the streets who has concerns, can report them to StreetLink. articles.title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
articles.excerpt: ‘Cruckle’ is the local verb for rolling or twisting an ankle — an old dialect survival that Rochdale speakers still recognise as a hometown word.
articles.summary: ‘Cruckle’ is the local verb for rolling or twisting an ankle — an old dialect survival that Rochdale speakers still recognise as a hometown word.
articles.body:
If you’ve ever heard someone in Rochdale say “I cruckled my ankle”, you haven’t misheard an idiosyncratic family coinage. In everyday local use the verb describes that awkward roll or twist of a foot — the sort of stumble you can usually walk off but which leaves you nursing a twinge. Contemporary perceptual-dialect research shows the word is not only used locally but also widely reported by people who explicitly link it to Rochdale speech. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

That research — a 2024 study of folk‑linguistic labels and map‑based perceptions across Greater Manchester — recorded respondents naming “cruckle” among the handful of words they associate with Rochdale when asked to characterise local speech. In the paper’s sample comments the term sits alongside other locally salient items such as guinnel (ginnel) and the label “broad”, which together paint the way people think about where they live and how it sounds. The study therefore gives us two linked facts: cruckle appears in local speech, and people perceive it as a Rochdale marker. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

But the word is not a modern invention. Historical dialect sources trace it to an older northern English verb‑group usually written crookle (and attested in variant spellings), with senses such as “to bend, make crooked, stoop” and extensions to hobbling or walking awkwardly. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect lexicography records crookle in northern and midland counties; linguists treat forms like crookle/cruckle as part of a broader crook/krug family across northern English and Scots dialects. That family’s basic image is simple: a hook‑like or bent motion, frequently expressed with an imitative or frequentative ‑le ending. ([en.wiktionary.org](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Template%3AR%3AEnglish_Dialect_Dictionary/documentation))

The Dictionary of the Scots Language records cognate forms explicitly: kruggle, cruggle and cruckle appear in Scots material with meanings such as “to crouch, bow down, huddle” — semantic cousins of the English crookle senses. Those Scots citations underline two points the dictionaries and comparative work make clear: first, the root is old and part of a northern dialect network; second, similar forms show up in adjacent speech areas (Scotland, northern England, some Scandinavian dialects), so the etymology is regional rather than uniquely local. articles.title: Failsworth tram stop lifts out of service during replacement works
articles.excerpt: Passengers at Failsworth tram stop face disruptions as lifts are out of service, affecting access to services towards Rochdale and East Didsbury.
articles.content_html:
Passengers using Failsworth tram stop are currently facing disruptions as both lifts are out of service due to ongoing replacement works. This situation affects access to services heading towards Rochdale and East Didsbury.

The lift on the platform heading to Rochdale is unavailable, and there is no step-free access at this stop. Passengers are advised to travel to Hollinwood tram stop to connect to services.

Customers requiring step-free access are encouraged to contact the Metrolink customer service centre for journey planning support. The contact number is 0161 244 1000, with lines open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

This lift outage is expected to continue until further notice, impacting those who rely on step-free access at Failsworth tram stop.

  • Travel times may be affected as passengers reroute to connect to services.
  • Customers needing assistance should contact Metrolink customer service before travelling.

articles.title: M62 closed near Milnrow after lorry hits central reservation
articles.excerpt: The M62 was closed near junction 21 at Milnrow on Sunday afternoon after a lorry hit the central reservation, the Lancashire Telegraph reported.
articles.content_html:
The M62 was closed near junction 21 at Milnrow on Sunday afternoon, 15 November, after a lorry hit the central reservation, cutting off a main route for Rochdale drivers.

The Lancashire Telegraph reported the closure in a live report it shared at about 4.20pm.

Junction 21 serves Milnrow, Newhey and Shaw. It is the last junction before the M62 climbs to junction 22 on the Pennines.

It was not yet confirmed which carriageway was closed, whether anyone was hurt, or when the motorway would reopen.

The same stretch, between junctions 22 and 21, was closed westbound on 10 and 11 October after a serious crash involving several vehicles.

Drivers can check live closures and diversions on National Highways' traffic information service before setting off.

This story will be updated as National Highways and the emergency services confirm details.
